normal-distribution-s1.title: Battery life of a phone model
normal-distribution-s1.text: Under a standard test, the battery life of a new phone model is approximately normal with mean 18 hours and standard deviation 1.5 hours (invented data). Let B = the battery life of a randomly chosen phone.

plot.label: Normal density curve of battery life with mean 18 hours and standard deviation 1.5 hours, the area below 16 hours shaded

normal-distribution-s2.title: Egg weights at a farm
normal-distribution-s2.text: The weights of eggs from a farm's hens are approximately normal with mean 58 grams and standard deviation 4 grams (invented data).

plot.label: Normal density curve of egg weights with mean 58 grams and standard deviation 4 grams, marked at 50, 54, 58, 62 and 66 grams

items.q: What is the probability that a randomly chosen phone's battery lasts less than 16 hours?

why.correct: B is $N(18, 1.5)$. $z = \frac{16 - 18}{1.5} \approx -1.33$, and $P(B < 16) = P(Z < -1.33) \approx 0.0912$ (technology gives 0.0912; Table A gives 0.0918).
options: That is the area to the right of 16 hours, the complement.
That uses the empirical rule for 1 standard deviation, but 16 hours is 1.33 standard deviations below the mean.
Right: the area to the left of z = −1.33.
That is the empirical rule for 2 standard deviations; 16 hours is less than 2 SDs away.

items.q: About what percent of phones have a battery life of more than 20.5 hours?

options: That is the area below 20.5 hours.
That is the empirical rule for 1 SD; 20.5 is 1.67 SDs above the mean.
That would be more than 2 SDs above the mean, 21 hours.
Right: the area to the right of z = 1.67.
About 95.2%
About 16%
About 2.5%
About 4.8%

items.q: What battery life is the 90th percentile?

why.correct: The 90th percentile has 0.90 of the area below it: $z \approx 1.28$, so $18 + 1.28(1.5) \approx 19.92$ hours.
options: Right: 1.28 standard deviations above the mean.
That is the 10th percentile, 1.28 SDs below the mean.
That uses z = 0.9 in place of the z-score with 0.90 of the area below it.
That is 2 standard deviations above the mean, about the 97.7th percentile.
19.92 hours
16.08 hours
19.35 hours
21.00 hours

items.q: By the empirical rule, about what percent of eggs weigh between 54 and 62 grams?

why.correct: 54 and 62 are 1 standard deviation below and above the mean, $58 \pm 4$, so about 68% of eggs fall between them.
options: That is within 2 standard deviations, 50 to 66 grams.
Right: within 1 standard deviation.
That is one side only, 58 to 62 grams.
Half of the eggs are below the mean, 58 grams.
About 95%
About 68%
About 34%
About 50%

items.q: By the empirical rule, about what percent of eggs weigh more than 66 grams?

why.correct: 66 is 2 standard deviations above the mean. About 95% lie within 2 SDs, leaving 5% in the two tails, so about 2.5% above 66 grams.
options: That is both tails together; above 66 is one tail.
That is above 1 SD, 62 grams.
Right: half of the 5% outside 2 SDs.
That is above 3 SDs, 70 grams.
About 5%
About 16%
About 2.5%
About 0.15%

items.q: What is the z-score of a 63-gram egg?

why.correct: $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} = \frac{63 - 58}{4} = 1.25$: the egg is 1.25 standard deviations above the mean.

mistakes.why: The sign is backward: value minus mean, so an egg above the mean has a positive z-score.
That is the distance in grams. Divide by the standard deviation, 4.

items.q: What is the probability that a randomly chosen egg weighs between 55 and 60 grams?

mistakes.why: That is the area below 60 grams. Subtract the area below 55.
Areas between two values subtract: the area below 60 minus the area below 55.

items.q: Write the expression for the z-score of a 50-gram egg.

mistakes.why: Subtract in the order value minus mean, so a light egg gets a negative z-score.
Divide by the standard deviation, 4, not its square.

items.q: Which is true of every density curve?

why.correct: A density curve is on or above the horizontal axis and has a total area of exactly 1 under it. Areas under it are probabilities (or proportions).
options: Normal curves are; other density curves can be skewed.
The area, not the height, is 1.
Right: areas are probabilities.
That holds for symmetric curves, not skewed ones.
It is symmetric and bell-shaped
Its highest point is at a height of 1
It lies on or above the axis and has a total area of 1 under it
Its mean and median are equal

items.q: Egg weights are modeled as $N(58, 4)$. What is the probability that a randomly chosen egg weighs exactly 60 grams?

why.correct: For a continuous model, probability is area, and a single value has no width, so its probability is 0. Questions ask about intervals, such as between 59.5 and 60.5 grams.
options: Heights of a density curve are not probabilities.
That is the probability of 60 grams or less.
Being near the mean does not give a single value half the area.
Right: only intervals have area.
The height of the curve at 60 grams
About 0.69, the area below 60 grams
About 0.5, because 60 is close to the mean
0, because a single value has no area under the curve

items.q: For the standard normal distribution, find $P(Z > 1.5)$.

mistakes.why: That is the area to the left of 1.5. "Greater than" is the right tail.
That uses the empirical rule for 1 SD; 1.5 is farther out.

items.q: For the standard normal distribution, what z-score has 25% of the area to its left (the first quartile)?

why.correct: Inverse normal: the z with area 0.25 to its left is about −0.67.

mistakes.why: That has 25% of the area to its right. The first quartile is below the mean, so z is negative.
That is the area. Find the z-score that has that area to its left.

items.q: An egg weighs 63 grams, so its z-score is 1.25 (mean 58 grams, standard deviation 4 grams). Build an interpretation of the z-score in context.

why.correct: A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, and in which direction.

claim.label: Meaning
options: The egg weighs 1.25 standard deviations more than the mean weight
The egg weighs 1.25 grams more than the mean weight
1.25% of eggs weigh more than this egg

why.1: The distance in grams is 5; 1.25 is in standard deviations.
why.2: A z-score is a position, not a percent.

context.label: Of what
options: of 58 grams for eggs from this farm
of all the eggs in the world
of a standard normal egg

why.1: The model describes this farm's eggs.
why.2: Name the real context and its units.

conclude.model: This 63-gram egg weighs 1.25 standard deviations more than the mean weight of 58 grams for eggs from this farm.

items.q: A histogram of the times 200 customers spent waiting at a bank is strongly skewed right. Should a normal model be used to find the percent who waited more than 10 minutes?

why.correct: A normal model fits only distributions that are roughly symmetric and mound-shaped. Strong right skew means normal areas would give wrong percents; use the data directly.
options: A large data set keeps its own shape; it does not become normal.
Knowing them does not make the shape normal.
Times can be close to normal; the problem here is the skew.
Right: check the shape before using a normal model.
Yes: any data set with 200 values can be treated as normal
Yes: the mean and standard deviation of the waits are known
No: a normal model is used for heights and not for times
No: the waits are strongly skewed, so normal areas would be wrong

items.q: The heaviest 5% of eggs are sold as "jumbo". Using $N(58, 4)$ grams, what is the minimum weight for a jumbo egg?

why.correct: The boundary has 0.95 of the area below it: $z \approx 1.645$, so $58 + 1.645(4) \approx 64.6$ grams.

mistakes.why: That is the lightest 5%: the boundary is above the mean for the heaviest eggs.
That uses the empirical rule (2 SDs), which leaves about 2.5% above, not 5%.

items.q: Ana scored 82 on a history test whose scores were approximately $N(70, 8)$. Ben scored 90 on a math test whose scores were approximately $N(80, 5)$. Who did better relative to the other students on the test?

why.correct: Compare z-scores: Ana $\frac{82 - 70}{8} = 1.5$, Ben $\frac{90 - 80}{5} = 2$. Ben is farther above his test's mean, in standard deviations.
options: Points mean different things on tests with different spreads.
Right: 2 standard deviations above the mean beats 1.5.
Raw scores on different tests cannot be compared directly.
Both are above the mean, but by different numbers of SDs.
Ana, because she was 12 points above her test's mean
Ben, whose z-score is 2 compared with Ana's 1.5
Ben, because 90 is a higher score than 82
They did equally well, since both scored above the mean
